q: There are no speed limit signs on a Saskatchewan highway. What is the speed limit?
o: 80 km/h
90 km/h
100 km/h
60 km/h
ex: In the absence of signs, the speed limit is 80 km/h.

q: What does a posted speed limit mean?
o: The fastest you may travel under ideal conditions
A safe speed in any weather or road condition
The speed you must keep when traffic is light
A guide you may exceed briefly while passing
ex: The speed limit is the fastest you can travel under ideal conditions. You must never drive faster than conditions allow.

q: A tow truck is stopped on the roadside with amber lights flashing, helping a disabled vehicle. What is your maximum speed when passing it?
o: 60 km/h
40 km/h
80 km/h
No limit if you change lanes
ex: Drivers must slow to 60 km/h when passing a tow truck stopped with amber (or amber and blue) lights flashing.

q: An emergency vehicle is stopped with its lights on, on the other side of a divided highway. Must you slow to 60 km/h?
o: No — it doesn't apply to the opposite side of a divided highway
Yes — the 60 km/h rule applies to both sides of every highway, divided or not
Yes — but only if officers are outside the vehicle
No — the 60 km/h rule applies only on city streets
ex: The 60 km/h rule doesn't apply to vehicles going the opposite way on a divided highway. It does apply on an undivided highway.

q: A snow plow is moving along the highway, clearing snow. Which is correct?
o: You may pass it when safe; the 60 km/h limit does not apply
You must not pass a snow plow while it is moving
You must slow to 60 km/h while passing it
You may pass it only on the right shoulder
ex: Moving snow plows may be passed when it's safe, without the 60 km/h limit. The 60 km/h limit applies when plows are stopped with blue and amber lights flashing.

q: What is the maximum speed when passing Ministry of Highways equipment with its lights flashing?
o: 60 km/h, whether it is moving or not
60 km/h, but only when it is stopped
80 km/h, whether it is moving or not
40 km/h, but only if workers are present
ex: When passing Ministry of Highways and Infrastructure equipment with lights flashing, moving or not, the maximum is 60 km/h.

q: You are driving through a school zone that has no speed signs. What should you do?
o: Still reduce your speed and proceed cautiously
Drive at 30 km/h, as set by provincial law
Drive normally — without signs no limit applies
Slow down only during recess and lunch hours
ex: School zone limits are set by local bylaws. If there are no signs, you should still reduce your speed and proceed cautiously.

q: Who receives a photo radar speeding ticket?
o: The registered owner of the vehicle
The driver, once identified from the photo
The person who renewed the registration
The insurance company of the vehicle
ex: Photo radar tickets are issued to the registered owner of the speeding vehicle.

q: Is it acceptable to drive so slowly that you hold up other traffic?
o: No — driving too slowly can be hazardous and must not block traffic
Yes — driving slower is always the safer choice for everyone
Yes — but only on highways, never on city streets
Yes — as long as you keep at least 40 km/h on the highway
ex: Travelling too slowly can be hazardous. Never drive slow enough to impede or block traffic unless proper safety precautions are taken.

q: Which offence leads to a 30-day vehicle impoundment?
o: Speeding 50 km/h or more over the posted limit
Speeding 30 km/h or more over the posted limit
Speeding 20 km/h over the limit in a work zone
Any speeding ticket within 12 months of another
ex: Excessive speeding — 50 km/h or more over the limit, or double the limit — results in a 30-day impoundment.

q: You are a learner (in the GDL program). May you use a hands-free cellphone while driving?
o: No — GDL drivers may not use any cellphone, even hands-free
Yes — if it is activated by voice commands
Yes — if it is mounted on the dashboard
Yes — hands-free use is allowed if the supervising driver sits beside you
ex: Hands-free cellphones are prohibited for drivers in the GDL program. Only experienced drivers may use hands-free devices.

q: Which cellphone use is allowed for a new (GDL) driver?
o: Calling 9-1-1 while driving
A hands-free call on a dash-mounted phone
A one-touch speakerphone call
Reading a text message at a red light
ex: Both new and experienced drivers may call 9-1-1 while driving, or make a call when parked on the side of the road.

q: Which cellphone use is allowed for an experienced driver?
o: A voice-activated call on a phone in a dash or visor mount
Holding the phone with the speakerphone on
Texting while stopped at a red light, as the vehicle is not moving
Viewing a map on a phone held in your hand
ex: Holding, viewing or manipulating a hand-held phone is prohibited. Experienced drivers may use hands-free phones activated by voice or one touch and mounted on the dash, visor or a cradle.

q: A driver with a cellphone conviction in the past 12 months gets another ticket for using a hand-held phone. What happens?
o: The vehicle is impounded for 7 days, even if someone else owns it
The vehicle is impounded for 30 days
The vehicle is impounded only if the driver owns it
Only a fine is issued; vehicles are impounded only for a third offence in a year
ex: A second offence within 12 months results in the vehicle being impounded for seven days, regardless of who owns it.

q: As a learner (Class 7), where must your supervising driver sit?
o: In the front passenger seat, at all times
Anywhere in the vehicle, at all times
In the front seat, only after dark
Behind the driver, if the front seat is taken
ex: A learner must have a supervising driver in the front passenger seat at all times — the seat nearest to the driver and controls.

q: Which person may act as a learner's supervising driver?
o: An experienced driver who held a valid licence 365 days in the last 3 years
A Novice 2 driver who has held a licence for over a year
Any adult with a Class 7 licence and 9 months of practice
Any adult aged 25 or older, whatever their licence class or history
ex: The supervisor must hold a Class 5 or greater licence, have held it at least 365 days in the past three years, and not be a novice driver.

q: How long must you practise with a learner's licence before you can take the road test?
o: Nine months
Six months
12 months
Three months
ex: The GDL program: Learner (Class 7) for nine months, then Novice 1 for six months, then Novice 2 for 12 incident-free months.

q: A Novice 2 driver has an at-fault collision. What happens to their 12-month period?
o: It restarts from the date of the collision
It continues; only convictions restart it
It is extended by three months
It restarts only after a second incident
ex: If a Novice 2 driver is at fault in a collision or convicted of a traffic offence, the 12-month incident-free period restarts from that date.

q: What blood alcohol content (BAC) is allowed for a new driver (learner or novice)?
o: Zero — any detectable amount leads to a suspension
Less than .04 — the same limit as experienced drivers
Less than .05 — a lower limit than for experienced drivers
Less than .08 — the Criminal Code limit applies to everyone
ex: There is zero tolerance for alcohol for new drivers, and zero tolerance for drugs for all drivers.

q: For an experienced driver, provincial roadside consequences start at what BAC?
o: Over .04
Over .05
Over .08
Any detectable amount
ex: Experienced drivers with a BAC over .04 (up to .08), or impaired by drugs, lose their licence and face other consequences.

q: At what BAC does driving become a Criminal Code offence?
o: 0.08 or more
0.04 or more
0.05 or more
0.10 or more
ex: It is a Criminal Code offence to drive with 80 mg or more of alcohol per 100 ml of blood (.08).

q: What removes alcohol from your body?
o: Only time
Black coffee and fresh air
A few hours of sleep
A large meal and water
ex: Only time can eliminate alcohol from the body. You cannot sleep off heavy drinking in a few hours.

q: Approximately how fast does alcohol leave the body?
o: .015% BAC per hour
.15% BAC per hour
.05% BAC per hour
.015% BAC per drink
ex: Alcohol leaves the system at about .015% per hour. Someone at .25% at midnight may still be over the limit at 10 a.m.

q: Two drinks combined with an antihistamine (cold remedy) can impair you about as much as...
o: 4 to 5 drinks
2 drinks — the medicine adds nothing
About 3 drinks
About 6 drinks
ex: Alcohol and drugs have a synergistic (multiplying) effect. Two drinks plus an antihistamine equal about 4 to 5 drinks. With Valium or Gravol, about 6.

q: What does alcohol affect first?
o: Judgment — the ability to think clearly and make decisions
Muscle control — balance and coordination
Vision — the small muscles of the eye
Reaction time — braking and steering slow down before anything else
ex: Alcohol first affects the brain's judgment, usually without the drinker noticing. Muscle control is affected second.

q: A tired driver drinks coffee to stay awake. What does the handbook say?
o: Its effect can wear off suddenly; the only remedy is to stop and sleep
It restores full alertness for the next several hours of driving
It is safe as long as you also open a window for fresh air
It works well if you keep drinking a cup every hour
ex: Stimulants like caffeine can wear off suddenly. The only remedy for fatigue is to pull off the road and sleep.

q: A medication label warns against operating heavy machinery. What does that mean for driving?
o: Treat it as a warning not to drive
It applies only to trucks and farm equipment
You may drive if you feel fine
You may drive short distances in town
ex: If the label advises against operating heavy machinery, consider it a warning not to get behind the wheel.

q: You stop on a rural road. How far must you be from a vehicle stopped on the opposite side?
ex: When stopping on a rural road or highway you must be 30 m (98 ft.) away from any vehicle stopped on the opposite side.

q: A vehicle is stopped on a highway at night. How must it be marked?
o: With flares, hazard lights or reflectors
With high-beam headlights left on
Only with the hood raised, so other drivers know it has broken down
It must be moved to the left shoulder
ex: Vehicles stopped on rural roads or highways at night must be marked with flares, hazard lights or reflectors.

q: Traffic is heavy and you must stop in your lane near an intersection. Where should you stop?
o: Behind the crosswalk, before entering the intersection
Inside the intersection, to keep your place
On the crosswalk, as long as no pedestrians are crossing at the time
Past the railway crossing, to keep traffic moving
ex: Always stop behind the crosswalk, before entering an intersection or before a railway crossing, so you don't obstruct pedestrians or traffic.

q: You are stopping for the stop sign at this intersection. Where must you stop?
o: At the clearly marked stop line
At the edge of the cross street
Beside the stop sign post
Past the line, where you can see both ways
ex: Where there is a clearly marked stop line, you must stop at it.

q: There is no stop line at this intersection. Where must you stop?
o: At the nearest crosswalk, marked or not
In the crosswalk, at the curb line
At the edge of the cross street, after you have passed the crosswalk
Within 10 m of the stop sign
ex: You must stop at the nearest crosswalk, whether it is marked or not.

q: At this rural intersection there is no stop line, sidewalk or crosswalk. Where must you stop?
o: Within 10 m of the intersection
Within 3 m of the intersection
Within 30 m of the intersection
Exactly beside the stop sign
ex: Where there is no stop line, sidewalk or crosswalk: within 3 m of the intersection in a town, city, village or hamlet, and within 10 m in a rural area.

q: In a town, with no stop line, sidewalk or crosswalk, where must you stop at a stop sign?
o: Within 3 m of the intersection
Within 10 m of the intersection
Within 5 m of the intersection
Wherever you can see best
ex: In a town, city, village or hamlet you must stop within three metres of the intersection when there are no markings.

q: Police signal you to stop. What must you do?
o: Pull over close to the right edge and stop before the next intersection
Keep driving slowly to a safe, well-lit spot several blocks away, then stop
Drive on to the nearest parking lot, then stop there
Pull over to the left shoulder and stop right away
ex: Pull over as close to the right-hand edge of the road as possible and stop before entering the next intersection.

q: Police ask for your licence and registration, but you don't have them with you. What may happen?
o: Police may allow you up to 48 hours to produce them
Your vehicle is impounded on the spot
You have up to 7 days to bring them
You must leave the vehicle until someone brings them
ex: If you don't have them with you, police may allow you up to 48 hours to produce them.

q: You have just passed a large truck. When is it safe to pull back in front of it?
o: When you can see the entire truck cab in your rear-view mirror
As soon as your rear bumper has cleared the truck's front bumper
When you see its headlights in your side mirror
When the truck driver flashes the headlights
ex: Truck drivers sit high and the hood hides part of the road. Pull in only when you can see the whole cab in your rear-view mirror.

q: The red areas around this large truck show its large blind spots. What does the handbook call them?
o: The no-zone
The closed gate
The safety cushion
The buffer zone
ex: The no-zone refers to the blind-spot areas around big trucks, where crashes are most likely to occur.

q: You are following a large truck. You can't see its side mirrors. What does that mean?
o: The truck driver can't see you
You are at a safe following distance
The truck driver sees you on the rear camera
You are too far back to be in danger
ex: A good rule of thumb: if you can't see the truck's mirrors, the truck driver can't see you.

q: A large truck is making a sharp right turn. What should you do?
o: Give it the room it needs and stay well back
Pass it on the right while it swings left
Pull up beside it at the curb
Sound your horn so it knows you are there
ex: Large trucks and buses have difficulty with sharp right turns. Give them room; vehicles on their right should stay well back to avoid being crushed against the curb.

q: An emergency vehicle with lights flashing and siren on approaches from behind. What must you do?
o: Pull close to the right edge and not enter the next intersection until it passes
Stop right where you are, even in the middle of an intersection, and wait
Speed up to clear the next intersection before it arrives
Pull to the left edge so it can pass you on the right
ex: Immediately drive as close as possible to the right edge and do not enter the next intersection until the emergency vehicle has passed.

q: You are on a one-way street when an emergency vehicle approaches with siren on. Where do you pull over?
o: To the nearest curb, right or left
Always pull to the right curb, even on a one-way street
Always to the left curb
Stay in your lane and stop
ex: On one-way streets, pull right or left to the nearest curb.

q: An ambulance passes you on the way to an emergency. May you follow it?
o: No — never follow an emergency vehicle to or from an emergency
Yes — as long as you stay at least 150 m behind it the whole way
Yes — if a police officer waves you through
Yes — it helps you get through traffic faster
ex: Never attempt to follow an emergency vehicle going to, or coming from, an emergency.

q: How fast does farm equipment usually travel on highways?
o: 10 to 40 km/h
40 to 60 km/h
5 to 15 km/h
30 to 50 km/h
ex: Farm equipment travels very slowly — 10 to 40 km/h — so you may come upon it very quickly.

q: A school bus ahead has its red lights flashing and stop arm out. How close may you stop?
o: No closer than 5 m from the bus
No closer than 3 m from the bus
No closer than 10 m from the bus
No closer than 15 m from the bus
ex: You must stop no closer than 5 m (15 ft.) from the front or back of the bus.

q: You meet a school bus with red lights flashing, coming from the opposite direction on an undivided highway. What must you do?
o: Stop as well
Slow down and pass with caution
Stop only if you see children
Continue — only traffic behind the bus stops
ex: If you approach the bus from the opposite direction on an undivided highway, you must also stop.

q: A school bus with red lights flashing is on the opposite side of a divided highway. What must you do?
o: You don't have to stop
You must stop, as on any highway
You must slow to 60 km/h
Stop only if children are crossing
ex: You don't have to stop for a school bus if you're travelling in the opposite direction on a divided highway.

q: A school bus ahead has amber (yellow) lights flashing. What should you do?
o: Slow down and proceed with caution
Stop at least 5 m from the bus
Pass quickly before the red lights come on
Stop only if the stop arm is out
ex: Amber flashing lights: slow down and proceed with caution. Red flashing lights: come to a complete stop.

q: You stopped for a school bus with red lights flashing. When may you move?
o: After the driver turns off the red lights and stop arm, and children have crossed
As soon as the stop arm starts to fold back, even if lights still flash
When the children reach the sidewalk, even if lights still flash
After waiting 30 seconds with the red lights flashing
ex: Do not advance until the bus driver turns off the flashing red lamps and deactivates the stop arm. Then check that all children have crossed.

q: What is the minimum fine for passing a school bus with red lights flashing?
ex: Passing a school bus with red flashing lights is a serious offence with a minimum fine of $360.

q: A school bus is stopped with only its four-way hazard lamps on. What must you do?
o: You're not required to stop, but go slowly and watch for children
Stop at least 5 m away, exactly as you would for flashing red lights
Stop only if the bus is on your side of the road
Pass at your normal speed — hazard lamps don't apply to you
ex: Drivers aren't required to stop for buses displaying four-way hazard lamps, but must use caution, go slowly and watch for children.

q: A motorcycle is riding on the left side of a wide lane. May you drive beside it in the same lane?
o: No — never move into the same lane beside a motorcycle
Yes — if the lane is wide enough and the rider stays to one side
Yes — if the rider waves you through
Yes — at low speeds in the city
ex: Never move into the same lane beside a motorcycle, even if the lane is wide. It's illegal and extremely hazardous.

q: A motorcycle shows a red 'L' or a green 'N' placard. What does it mean?
o: A learner or novice rider — give them plenty of space
L means a licensed rider, and N means night riding is allowed
A large or normal engine size
L = loaded with a passenger, N = no passenger
ex: New motorcyclists display a red 'L' (learner) or green 'N' (novice) placard. Use caution and give them plenty of space.

q: During motorcycle season, how should you check before a lane change or turn?
o: Check twice — once for cars and trucks, once for motorcycles and bikes
Check your mirrors once — motorcycles always have their headlights on
Check only the inside mirror
Sound your horn before moving over
ex: Check twice before a lane change or turn — once for cars and trucks, and once for motorcycles and bikes.

q: You are turning left and a cyclist is coming toward you. What must you do?
o: Stop and wait for the oncoming bicycle to pass before turning
Turn first — on a left turn, bicycles must yield to motor vehicles
Turn if the cyclist is in a bike lane
Sound your horn and complete the turn
ex: When turning left, you must stop and wait for oncoming bicycles to pass before turning.

q: Should you use your horn when passing a cyclist?
o: No — not unnecessarily; it may frighten them into your path
Yes — always give one short honk so the cyclist knows you are there
Yes — honk twice on highways where speeds are higher
Only at night, when they can't see you coming from behind
ex: Don't unnecessarily use your horn when passing a cyclist. It may frighten them and cause them to steer into your path.

q: You need to turn right at a corner where there is a bicycle-only lane. What is correct?
o: Enter the bike lane when it is safe, then make the turn
Turn from your lane; never enter a bike lane
Drive in the bike lane for the whole block first
Turn ahead of cyclists — they must stop for you
ex: Vehicles may enter a bicycle-only lane to make a right turn. Enter only after making sure it's safe, then turn.

q: What does a 'sharrow' (bicycle symbol with chevrons painted in the lane) mean?
o: Cyclists and motorists share the lane — it is not a bike lane
The lane is reserved for bicycles only, like a bike lane
Cyclists must ride on the arrow in the centre
Cars may pass cyclists within the lane at any time
ex: Sharrows encourage cyclists and motorists to share the lane. They do not designate a bicycle lane, and you should still pass cyclists at a safe distance.

q: Where e-scooters are allowed, how old must riders be?
o: At least 16, wearing an approved helmet
At least 14, wearing a helmet
At least 18, with a driver's licence
Any age, if they stay in bike lanes
ex: E-scooter users don't need a licence or registration, but must be at least 16 years old and wear an approved helmet.

q: How should you treat a funeral procession?
o: Don't interrupt it; it must still obey signals unless drivers with the right of way stop
It has the right of way through red lights, just like an ambulance
Pass it as quickly as possible on the left to clear the road
Join the end of it so you can get through the intersection too
ex: Funeral processions should not be interfered with. They must obey all traffic signs and signals, unless all drivers with the right of way stop to let them proceed.

q: You see a snowmobile near the road. What should you expect?
o: It may cross the road suddenly or go out of control
It must yield to you, so you can keep your speed
Snowmobiles are easy to see in storms
It will always wait for traffic to clear
ex: Snowmobiles are small, low and hard to see, often out in poor visibility, sometimes driven by children. Anticipate that one may cross suddenly or go out of control.

q: Imagine four 'gates' around your vehicle. How many open gates should a safe driver always try to keep?
o: At least two
At least one
All four
At least three
ex: A safe driver always tries to have at least two open gates to provide options for emergency movement.

q: A vehicle behind you is tailgating. Your rear gate is closed. What should you do?
o: Increase your following distance ahead to five or six seconds
Speed up to open a bigger gap between you and the tailgater
Tap the brakes firmly a few times to warn the other driver
Move onto the shoulder and stay there until it passes you
ex: If you're being tailgated, leave extra distance ahead so you have room to stop — increase it to five or six seconds.

q: How do you check the blind spot before moving into a side gate?
o: A quick shoulder check toward the gate you are moving into
Look in the inside mirror a second time before moving
Check the inside mirror and both outside mirrors before moving
Rely on the blind spot warning light if the car has one
ex: A blind spot can't be seen in any mirror. A quick glance over your shoulder toward the gate you're moving into lets you see it.

q: You notice you are driving in another driver's blind spot. What should you do?
o: Move forward or drop back as soon as you notice
Stay beside them and sound your horn so they know you're there
Flash your headlights so they know
Match their speed to stay visible
ex: Don't drive in other drivers' blind spots. Move forward, or drop back, as soon as you notice.

q: What do yellow lines on the road separate?
o: Traffic travelling in opposite directions
Traffic travelling in the same direction
Parking lanes from driving lanes
Bus lanes from regular lanes
ex: Yellow directional dividing lines separate traffic travelling in opposite directions. White lines separate traffic in the same direction.

q: You are driving in a lane marked with double wide lines. What does it mean?
o: The lane is ending — be ready to exit, turn or merge
The lane is for buses and taxis only
A new lane is being added ahead, so you may keep driving in it
Passing is permitted from this lane
ex: Lanes that are ending are usually marked with double wide lines. Be prepared to exit, turn at the next intersection or merge.

q: Vehicle A is behind vehicle B. The centre line is a single broken yellow line. May A pass?
o: Yes, if the road is clear ahead and behind
No — a yellow line always means no passing
Only on the right side of B
Only if B signals right first
ex: A broken line allows passing when it is safe — the road must be clear ahead and behind.

q: Vehicle A is behind vehicle B. There is a double line: broken on A's side, solid on the far side. May A pass?
o: Yes — the line nearest A is broken, if it's clear ahead and behind
No — any double line in the centre means passing is never allowed
Only if the solid line were on A's side
Yes — without checking, since A has the broken line
ex: You may not cross a solid line, except where the line nearest you is broken.

q: Vehicle A is behind vehicle B. The centre line is double solid yellow. What may A do?
o: A must not pass or turn left between intersections
A may pass if no traffic is coming
A may turn left into a driveway, but must not pass
A may pass if B is going under 40 km/h
ex: With a double solid line, vehicle A must not pass or make a left turn between intersections.

q: Vehicle A is behind vehicle B. There is a double line: solid on A's side, broken on the far side. May A pass?
o: No — the line nearest A is solid
Yes — the broken line allows passing
Yes — if the road is clear ahead
Only to pass slow farm equipment
ex: You may not move across a solid line. Here the line nearest vehicle A is solid, so A must not pass.

q: On highways and rural roads, where should you position your vehicle in the lane?
o: To the right of your lane
In the exact centre of the lane
To the left, near the centre line
Wherever traffic is lightest
ex: On highways or rural roads, keep to the right of your lane. In urban areas you usually drive in the middle of the lane.

q: What may the highway shoulder be used for?
o: Stopped vehicles, emergencies, and preparing for a right turn
An extra driving lane for slower traffic when traffic is heavy
Passing a vehicle that is turning left
Slow vehicles that want to let traffic by at speed
ex: The shoulder is for stopped vehicles, emergency manoeuvres, two-point turns or preparing a right turn. It's not an extra driving lane.

q: On a multi-lane divided highway, what is the left lane intended for?
o: Passing slower vehicles, and emergency vehicles
Any traffic that keeps up with the speed limit, at any time
Trucks and buses only
Slower vehicles, so they don't hold up the right lane
ex: On a multi-lane divided highway the left lane is for passing slower right-lane vehicles or for emergency vehicles.

q: At an intersection where signs show two lanes may turn, what must you do?
o: Complete the turn in the same relative lane position
Finish in any lane that is free
The outer lane must yield to the inner lane
Finish in the right lane, then move over
ex: Where two or more lanes may turn, approach and complete the turn in the same relative lane position.

q: When driving under 60 km/h, how far before a turn should you signal?
o: At least 30 m
At least 15 m
At least 60 m
At least 150 m
ex: Under 60 km/h signal at least 30 m before turning. At higher speeds, signal at least 150 m from the corner.

q: When driving at higher speeds (over 60 km/h), how far before the corner should you signal?
o: At least 150 m
At least 30 m
At least 100 m
At least 300 m
ex: At speeds over 60 km/h, signal at least 150 m from the corner.

q: What does this hand signal mean?
o: Left turn
Right turn
Stopping or slowing abruptly
You may pass me
ex: Left arm straight out: left turn. Arm bent up: right turn. Arm bent down: stopping or slowing abruptly.

q: What does this hand signal mean?
o: Right turn
Left turn
Stopping or slowing abruptly
Pull over to the right
ex: Left arm bent up at the elbow: right turn. These hand signals must be used if your signal or brake lights fail, and are also used by cyclists.

q: What does this hand signal mean?
o: Stopping or slowing abruptly
Right turn
Left turn
Please slow down behind me gradually
ex: Left arm bent down: stopping or slowing abruptly.

q: What is the correct order when you plan to change lanes?
o: Signal, check the mirror, shoulder check, then move
Check the mirror, start moving, then signal once you're in the lane
Shoulder check, move, then signal
Signal and move; check the mirror after
ex: The procedure: signal, check your mirror, shoulder check the blind spot, start the turn or lane change, then cancel the signal.

q: You want to change lanes as you approach an intersection. What should you do?
o: Finish the change before the intersection, or wait until you are through it
Change lanes inside the intersection, where there is more room
Signal in the intersection, then change lanes right after it
Change lanes while you cross the crosswalk, before the corner
ex: Complete your lane change and cancel your signal before entering the intersection, or wait until you're through it to signal and change lanes.

q: You need to move across more than one lane. What is correct?
o: Make it one continual action with one signal, shoulder checking each lane
Signal again and stop briefly between each lane you move across
Shoulder check only once, before you move into the first lane
Cross all the lanes at once, without checks, to be quick
ex: When moving through more than one lane, make the change as one continual action. Only one signal is needed, but shoulder check each lane change.

q: Where is passing NOT allowed?
o: On the crest of a hill or before a curve
On a straight road with a broken line
In a passing lane on a two-lane highway
On a divided highway with two lanes your way
ex: Don't pass on the crest of a hill, before a curve, at intersections, or anywhere your sight distance is limited. Don't cross solid lines.

q: While passing another vehicle, what does the handbook say about your speed?
o: Keep accelerating through the pass, but never exceed the speed limit
You may exceed the limit briefly so you spend less time passing
Slow down once you are beside the other vehicle
Hold the same speed as the vehicle you are passing
ex: Accelerate before and throughout the pass, but it's illegal to speed even when passing.

q: After passing, when may you return to your lane?
o: When you see the passed vehicle in your inside rear-view mirror
As soon as your rear bumper is a metre past its front bumper
When you can see it in your right side mirror
When its driver flashes the headlights to let you in
ex: Wait until you see the vehicle you passed in your inside rear-view mirror. Then signal, check mirrors and shoulder check before moving back.

q: On a two-lane road, when may you pass a vehicle on the right?
o: When it is about to turn left and you can pass without using the shoulder
Whenever the shoulder is wide and paved enough to drive on safely
Never — passing on the right is illegal in every situation
When it is going well below the posted speed limit
ex: You must pass on the left, except where there are two or more lanes in your direction, or when the vehicle ahead is turning left and you can pass safely without driving on the shoulder.

q: A vehicle ahead has stopped at an intersection to let pedestrians cross. May you pass it?
o: No — you may not pass it
Yes — on the left if the lane is clear
Yes — slowly, on the right
Yes — after sounding your horn
ex: You may not pass any vehicle that is stopped at an intersection to permit pedestrians to cross.

q: Another vehicle is passing you. What should you do?
o: Keep right and maintain your speed — do not speed up
Speed up a little so the other driver finishes the pass sooner
Brake hard so it can cut in quickly
Move onto the shoulder and stop
ex: When being passed, stay to the right of your lane and maintain your speed. Don't accelerate. If the passer misjudged, slow down and let them back in.

q: On a highway with a passing lane, which lane is the travel lane?
o: The right lane; the left lane is only for passing
The left lane; the right lane is for trucks
Either lane, as long as you keep to the limit
The right lane, but only for trucks and farm vehicles
ex: In a passing lane section, the right lane is for travel and the left lane is only for passing. When you move right, maintain your speed and don't speed up.

q: When estimating your safe passing time, what minimum safety margin should you add?
o: Five seconds
Two seconds
Three seconds
Ten seconds
ex: Your passing time + a minimum five-second safety margin = your safe passing time.

q: When passing a motorcycle, what should you keep in mind before returning to the lane?
o: Leave a greater distance — it's easy to underestimate due to its size
Leave less room than for a car — motorcycles are much shorter
Return as soon as you are past the motorcycle's rear wheel
Sound your horn so the rider moves over and lets you in
ex: When passing a motorcycle, leave a greater distance before pulling back into the lane. It's easy to underestimate how much room you need.

q: Bus lane hours are in effect. When may you drive in the bus lane?
o: Only to make a right turn onto or off that street
Whenever no bus can be seen coming up behind you
To pass slower traffic in the next lane
To drop off or pick up passengers
ex: During bus lane hours, only buses and emergency vehicles may use the lane, except vehicles making a right turn onto or off the block.

q: Vehicles are parked in the curb lane near the corner. How should you make a right turn?
o: Move into the curb lane at the first opportunity, then turn
Turn right from the main driving lane, around the parked cars
Wait behind the parked cars until they leave
Swing into the oncoming lane to turn wide
ex: When vehicles are parked in the curb lane near the intersection, move into that lane at the first opportunity before turning. You may not turn from the main driving lane.

q: You must stop in the intersection while waiting to turn left. How should your front wheels be?
o: Straight, with the vehicle parallel to the lane
Turned left, ready to make the turn
Turned right, toward the curb
It doesn't matter if you keep your foot on the brake
ex: Keep your vehicle parallel to the lane and the front wheels straight. If you're hit from behind, you won't be pushed into oncoming traffic.

q: You are turning left. Who must you yield to?
o: Oncoming vehicles close enough that your turn would interfere
Only oncoming vehicles in the left lane
No one, as long as you entered the intersection first
Only vehicles going faster than you
ex: When turning left, you must yield to any vehicles coming toward you if they are close enough that your turn would interfere with them.

q: You turn left from a one-way street onto a two-way street. Which lane do you enter?
o: The lane immediately to the right of the centre line
The curb lane on the far right
Any lane that is clear
The lane left of the centre line, then move over
ex: Turn from as close as possible to the left edge of the one-way street and enter the lane immediately to the right of the centre line.

q: You turn left from a two-way street onto a one-way street. How do you do it?
o: Turn from the lane next to the centre line into the left-most lane
Turn from the right lane into the right-most lane
Turn from any lane into any clear lane
Turn from the lane next to the centre line into the curb lane
ex: For a left turn from a two-way to a one-way street, turn from the lane next to the centre line and enter the left-most driving lane.

q: You turn left from a one-way street onto another one-way street. How do you do it?
o: Start from the left edge and finish in the left-most lane
Start from the centre lane and finish in the centre lane
Start from the right lane and finish in the left lane
Start from the left edge and finish in the right-most lane
ex: For a left turn from a one-way street to a one-way street, start the turn from the left edge of the roadway and complete it in the left-most driving lane.

q: Which is a major factor in collisions involving motorcycles?
o: Drivers turning left who fail to see an oncoming motorcycle
Motorcycles riding with their headlights on during the day
Motorcyclists riding two abreast in one lane
Drivers following motorcycles by four seconds
ex: Motorists failing to identify oncoming motorcycles when making a left turn is a significant contributing factor in motorcycle collisions.

q: When are U-turns allowed at an intersection with traffic lights?
o: Only if a sign shows U-turns are permitted
Whenever the light is green and traffic is clear
Only on a flashing amber light
Never, even with a sign
ex: You may not make a U-turn at any intersection with traffic lights unless a sign indicates U-turns are permitted.

q: You plan a U-turn in a 60 km/h area. How much clear sight distance do you need each way?
o: At least 20 seconds
At least 10 seconds
At least 40 seconds
At least 12 seconds
ex: In a 60 km/h area you need at least 20 seconds of sight time each way. In a 100 km/h area, 40 seconds.

q: Car A wants to turn left into a property using the centre turning lane. Where should it enter that lane?
o: Only at the point next to the property it wants to reach
As early as possible, to get out of the through traffic sooner
At least one block before the property
Anywhere, and drive in it until the property
ex: Enter the two-way left turning lane only at the point adjacent to the property you want to access.

q: May you use a centre turning lane to pass slower traffic?
o: No — it may not be used as a passing lane or a driving lane
Yes — for a short distance, as long as nobody is waiting to turn
Yes — but only to pass slow farm equipment
Yes — but only during rush hour
ex: Centre turning lanes may not be used as a passing lane or a driving lane. Where one is provided, you may not turn left from any other lane.

q: Car B is leaving a parking lot to turn left across a centre turning lane. What should it do?
o: Pick a gap, drive through the centre lane and into the first available lane quickly
Drive along in the centre lane until a gap opens in the traffic
Stop in the centre lane and wait there for as long as needed
Turn right first, then make a U-turn at the next light
ex: When leaving a driveway, pick a gap in traffic, complete the turn through the centre turning lane and into the first available driving lane as quickly as possible.

q: Two vehicles reach an uncontrolled intersection (no signs or lights) at about the same time. Who must yield?
o: The vehicle on the left yields to the vehicle on the right
The vehicle on the right yields to the vehicle on the left
The vehicle turning yields to the one going straight
The smaller vehicle yields to the larger one
ex: At an uncontrolled intersection, the driver on the left must yield the right of way to the driver on the right.

q: At an uncontrolled T-intersection, two vehicles arrive at about the same time. Which rule applies?
o: The same rule: yield to the vehicle on your right
The vehicle on the through road always goes first
The vehicle on the ending road always goes first
The first vehicle to signal goes first
ex: The 'yield to the vehicle on the right' rule also applies to T-intersections.

q: You are entering a provincial highway from a side road. Who must you yield to?
o: All vehicles on the highway and pedestrians closely approaching
Only vehicles approaching from your left, as they are closer
Only trucks and buses on the highway
No one, if the vehicle on the highway is on your left
ex: When entering a provincial highway from any other road, yield to any vehicles on the highway and to any pedestrian closely approaching the intersection.

q: You are driving out of an alley onto a street. Who must you yield to?
o: Pedestrians on the sidewalk and vehicles on the street
Only vehicles on the street
Only pedestrians on the sidewalk
No one, if the traffic on the street is coming from your left
ex: When entering a street from a private road, lane or alley, yield to pedestrians on the sidewalk and to vehicles on the street.

q: At a four-way stop, who goes first?
o: The first vehicle to stop; the others then yield to the driver on their right
The vehicle on the left goes first; the others then follow in turn
The largest vehicle goes first; others wait
Vehicles going straight always go before vehicles turning
ex: At three- and four-way stops, the first vehicle that stops gets the right of way. The others then yield to the driver on their right.

q: Two vehicles stop at the same time at opposite stop signs. One is turning left, the other going straight. Who goes first?
o: The vehicle going straight
The vehicle turning left
The vehicle that signalled first
The vehicle on the right of the other
ex: The driver turning left must yield to the driver going straight. If opposing vehicles are both going straight, they may proceed at the same time.

q: You are stopped at a two-way stop. When may you go?
o: Only after all cross traffic has passed and it is safe
When the cross traffic slows down and leaves you a gap
After waiting three seconds
When the vehicle on your left waves you on
ex: At two-way stops, vehicles must remain stopped until all cross traffic passes.

q: You have the right of way, but another driver refuses to yield. What should you do?
o: Avoid the collision rather than insist on your right of way
Continue — the other driver will be legally at fault for any crash
Sound your horn and proceed at the same speed
Flash your lights and go first
ex: All drivers have a moral and legal responsibility to avoid collisions. If a driver refuses to yield, you're responsible for avoiding a crash rather than insisting on your right of way.

q: When must you yield to highway construction or maintenance vehicles?
o: At all times when their warning lights are flashing
Only when they are stopped on the road with lights flashing
Only inside a marked work zone
Only during daylight hours
ex: At all times, you must yield the right of way to highway construction or maintenance vehicles with warning lights flashing.

q: A lane is closed ahead in a construction zone. How does a zipper merge work?
o: Use both lanes until the lane ends, then take turns merging
Merge into the open lane as early as possible, before the taper
Vehicles in the ending lane must stop and wait for a gap
Drivers in the open lane must not let anyone in
ex: A zipper merge means using both lanes until the lane ends, then alternating into the open lane. Each driver in the continuing lane should let one vehicle in.

q: You are entering a roundabout. Who must you yield to?
o: Traffic already in the roundabout
Traffic entering from your right
No one — entering traffic has priority
Only pedestrians at the crosswalk
ex: Traffic entering a roundabout must yield to traffic in the roundabout. In a roundabout, the vehicle on the right yields to the vehicle on the left.

q: In a two-lane roundabout you plan to go past the second exit. Which lane should you use?
o: The left lane
The right lane
Either lane
The right lane, then move left at the exit
ex: The right lane is mainly for exiting at the first exit. If you intend to go beyond the second exit, drive in the left lane.

q: What signal do you use when leaving a roundabout?
o: The right-turn signal
The left-turn signal
Your hazard lights
No signal is needed
ex: When leaving the roundabout, use your right-turn signal to warn other drivers that you intend to exit.

q: At a restricted crossing U-turn (RCUT) intersection, how do you cross the divided highway?
o: Turn right, then make a U-turn
Turn left directly across the median
Drive straight across when there is a gap
Make a U-turn first, then turn right
ex: At an RCUT you are not allowed to turn left or drive straight across. You turn right into the acceleration lane, move to the U-turn lane and make a U-turn.

q: In a diverging diamond interchange, after the traffic light you find yourself on the opposite side of the road. What does that mean?
o: It's normal — you'll cross back at the next light
You took a wrong turn and must stop and wait for help
You are in the wrong lane and must back up
You must turn left immediately
ex: In a diverging diamond, traffic crosses to the opposite side for a short distance and returns at the next signal. Don't panic; follow lane signs and markings.

q: The light changes while a pedestrian is still in the crosswalk. Who has the right of way?
o: The pedestrian
You, because your light is now green
The vehicle turning right
Whoever moves first
ex: If a traffic light changes while a pedestrian is in the crosswalk, the pedestrian has the right of way.

q: Where must you stop for pedestrians at an intersection without painted lines?
o: Before the crosswalk — an imaginary extension of the sidewalk
Anywhere before the centre of the intersection
Only where crosswalk lines are painted on the road surface
Past the sidewalk, at the curb line
ex: Stop before the crosswalk, which is either painted on the road or is an imaginary extension of the sidewalk.

q: There is no sidewalk. Where should pedestrians walk along the road?
o: On the left shoulder, facing oncoming traffic
On the right shoulder, travelling in the same direction as traffic
In the centre of the lane
On either shoulder
ex: Pedestrians walking along a road should walk on the left shoulder, facing oncoming traffic.

q: A pedestrian is waiting to jaywalk mid-block. What should you do?
o: Be prepared to stop, but don't stop and wave them across
Stop and wave them across — it is the polite and safe thing to do
Sound your horn and keep going
Speed up to pass before they step out
ex: Always be prepared to stop for a pedestrian stepping out, but don't encourage jaywalking — the car behind you may not expect you to stop, and other lanes may not see the pedestrian.

q: A school crossing guard signals you to stop at a crosswalk. What must you do?
o: Stop
Slow down and pass if no child is on the road
Stop only if children are already crossing
Proceed if your light is green
ex: You must stop your vehicle when directed to do so by a school crossing guard controlling a crosswalk.

q: Where may you drive across an urban street?
o: Only at an intersection, lane or alley
Anywhere there is a break in the median and no traffic
Anywhere, if no traffic is coming
Only at traffic lights
ex: You may drive across a street only at an intersection, lane or alley. Some cities prohibit crossing at a lane or alley by bylaw.

q: A road is divided by a median. Where may you cross it?
o: Only at an intersection or a provided cross-over
Anywhere the median is flat enough to drive across safely
Anywhere, to make a U-turn
Only in the daytime
ex: You may not cross any median, boulevard or ditch except at an intersection or where a cross-over is provided. You may not drive on the left side of it.

q: In this parking lot, car A and car B meet where two parking lanes cross with no signs. Who yields?
o: Car A yields to car B, the vehicle on its right
Car B yields to car A, because A arrived at the crossing first
The car that is turning yields
Whoever reaches a parking spot first
ex: When parking lanes intersect without yield or stop signs, treat it as an uncontrolled intersection — yield to the vehicle on the right.

q: Car C wants to drive from a parking lane onto the thoroughfare, where car D is travelling. Who yields?
o: Car C yields to car D on the thoroughfare
Car D yields to car C, because C is on its right
They follow the four-way stop rule
Whoever arrives first
ex: Thoroughfares lead into, through or out of a parking lot. Parking lanes and passageways must yield to thoroughfares.

q: When does the law require headlights to be on?
o: From half an hour after sunset to half an hour before sunrise, and in poor visibility
From sunset to sunrise only, whatever the visibility
From one hour after sunset until one hour before sunrise, and in fog
Only on highways outside city limits, from dusk to dawn
ex: Headlights are required from half an hour after sunset until half an hour before sunrise, and any time visibility is poor. Driving with lights on at all times is recommended.

q: You are using high beams and a vehicle is coming toward you. When must you dim them?
o: At least 200 m before the oncoming vehicle
At least 100 m before the oncoming vehicle
At least 500 m before the oncoming vehicle
Only when the oncoming driver flashes their lights at you
ex: Dim your high beams at least 200 m (650 ft.) in advance of oncoming vehicles and keep them dimmed until the vehicle has passed.

q: You are following another vehicle at night. When must you use low beams?
o: Within 100 m of the vehicle ahead
Within 200 m of the vehicle ahead
Within 50 m of the vehicle ahead
Only on curves, where your lights can shine into their mirrors
ex: You must keep your headlights on low beam within 100 m (330 ft.) when following another vehicle or when being passed.

q: How far before an oncoming vehicle must you turn off spotlamps or auxiliary driving lights?
o: At least 500 m
At least 200 m
At least 100 m
At least 1 km
ex: Turn off spotlamps at least 500 m (1,640 ft.) in advance of an oncoming vehicle.

q: When don't you need to dim your high beams for oncoming traffic?
o: On a divided highway where the roadways are 22 m or more apart
On any divided highway, whatever the distance between roadways
On gravel roads that have no painted centre line to divide traffic
When the oncoming driver doesn't dim their own high beams
ex: You don't need to dim for oncoming traffic on a divided highway where the distance between roadways is 22 m (70 ft.) or more.

q: At night with no street lights, how far ahead should you be able to see?
o: About 12 seconds of travel
About 3 seconds of travel
About 6 seconds of travel
About 30 seconds of travel
ex: At night you should be able to see about 12 seconds ahead, so most of the time you should use high beams and look beyond your lights.

q: At night you see something on the road ahead but can't tell what it is. What should you do?
o: Slow down immediately while you identify it
Keep your speed until you can see it clearly
Switch to low beams to see it better
Swerve into the other lane right away
ex: The most important action at night is to slow immediately when you detect something. Don't wait until you can see it clearly — by then it may be too late.

q: In fog, blowing snow or heavy rain, which headlights help you see better?
o: Low beams
High beams
Parking lights only
Hazard lights only
ex: In fog, blowing snow or heavy rain you will see better with your lights on low beam.

q: You have slowed down but still can't see 12 seconds ahead in heavy fog. What should you do?
o: Find a safe place as soon as you can and get off the road
Follow the tail lights of the vehicle ahead closely to keep on the road
Turn on high beams to see further
Stop in your lane with the hazards on
ex: If you've slowed down and still can't see 12 seconds ahead, find a safe place as soon as you can and get off the road.

q: When is the road most slippery during a rainstorm?
o: During the first 10 minutes
After an hour of steady rain
Only when the rain turns to hail
At the end of the storm
ex: During the first 10 minutes of a rainstorm, the roads are the most slippery.

q: You face a red light and want to turn right. No sign prohibits it. What must you do?
o: Stop, yield to pedestrians and traffic, then turn
Turn right on red only where a sign permits it
Wait for the green light
Slow down, then turn without stopping if the way is clear
ex: On a red light you may turn right after stopping and yielding to pedestrians and vehicles, unless a sign prohibits it.

q: You approach an amber (yellow) light. What must you do?
o: Stop before the crosswalk; if you can't stop safely, proceed with caution
Speed up so you can clear the intersection before the light turns red
Stop even if you are already inside the intersection
Treat it like a green light if no pedestrians are near
ex: At an amber light you must stop before entering the crosswalk. If you have already entered, or cannot stop safely, proceed with caution.

q: You approach a flashing red light. What must you do?
o: Stop, then proceed when it's safe
Slow down and proceed with caution
Stop and wait for it to turn green
Yield only to vehicles on your right
ex: At a flashing red light you must stop, but you may then proceed when it's safe — treat it like a stop sign.

q: You approach a flashing amber (yellow) light. What must you do?
o: Proceed with caution
Stop, then proceed when safe
Stop and wait for green
Speed up through the intersection
ex: When approaching a flashing amber light, you must proceed with caution.

q: You face a red light together with a solid green arrow. What may you do?
o: Go in the direction of the arrow after yielding to vehicles and pedestrians
Go in any direction, since a green arrow is showing
Wait — the red light means stop for all directions
Go in the direction of the arrow; other vehicles must yield to you
ex: With a red light and a solid green arrow, you may proceed in the direction of the arrow only after yielding to other vehicles and pedestrians.

q: After a flashing green left-turn arrow, an amber arrow appears. What does it mean?
o: The green light is about to appear for traffic in both directions
You must complete your left turn immediately, before it turns red
All traffic in every direction must stop now
Pedestrians may now cross in front of turning traffic
ex: After the left-turn arrow, an amber arrow may appear. It means the green light is about to appear for traffic in both directions.

q: You entered the intersection on a green light to turn left, but heavy oncoming traffic keeps coming. What does the handbook say?
o: You may complete the turn on an amber or red light
You must back out of the intersection
You must wait in the intersection for the next green
You must turn right instead
ex: If you entered on green to turn left and traffic is heavy, you may be forced to complete your turn on an amber or red light.

q: A pedestrian signal shows a flashing 'don't walk'. What does it mean for pedestrians?
o: Finish crossing if already started; don't start crossing
Start crossing quickly, before the signal turns to a steady 'don't walk'
Stop in the middle of the road
It is safe to cross at any pace
ex: A flashing 'don't walk' means pedestrians should finish crossing if they have already started.

q: What is the minimum following distance in ideal conditions?
o: Three seconds
Two seconds
One car length per 10 km/h
Five seconds
ex: Keep a minimum three-second following distance in ideal conditions. Increase it when conditions are less than ideal.

q: How do you measure your following distance?
o: Count seconds from when the vehicle ahead passes a fixed object until you reach it
Read the speedometer and divide the number by ten
Count car lengths: leave one car length for every 10 km/h of speed
Count the broken lines on the road between the two vehicles
ex: Pick a fixed object. When the back bumper of the vehicle ahead passes it, count 'thousand-one, thousand-two…' until your front bumper reaches it.

q: With a three-second following distance at 100 km/h, how far back are you compared with 50 km/h?
o: Twice as far
The same distance
Half as far
Four times as far
ex: A three-second gap automatically lengthens as you go faster: at 100 km/h you are twice as far back as at 50 km/h.

q: During the first few snowfalls of winter, what following distance should you keep?
o: Five seconds
Three seconds
Two seconds
Ten seconds
ex: During the first few snowfalls, drive very slowly and keep a five-second following distance.

q: You are following a large truck that blocks your view ahead. What should you do?
o: Drop back to more than three seconds until you can see around it
Follow closer so that you can see past the side of the truck
Pass it right away, before the view gets worse
Keep exactly three seconds, as in ideal conditions
ex: If a truck or van blocks your view, drop back to more than three seconds until you can see around it.

q: What does IPDE stand for?
o: Identify, Predict, Decide, Execute
Inspect, Plan, Drive, Evaluate — the four steps of a pre-trip check
Identify, Plan, Decide, Evaluate
Inspect, Predict, Determine, Execute
ex: IPDE — Identify, Predict, Decide, Execute — is the approach for dealing with real and potential hazards.

q: The circled truck is at the corner ahead and might pull out. What kind of hazard is it?
o: A potential hazard
A real hazard
Not a hazard until they step out
A fixed hazard
ex: A potential hazard is something that might happen: a pedestrian who might cross, a car that might pull out, a light that might change. A real hazard is one you have to react to now.

q: The circled pedestrian is crossing in front of you. What kind of hazard is it?
o: A real hazard
A potential hazard
Not a hazard if you are far back
A traffic condition, not a hazard
ex: A real hazard is something you have to react to — a stop light, a car stopping in your lane, a curve that requires you to slow down.

q: Another vehicle is approaching the same intersection. When you check again, it is still in the same position relative to you. What does that mean?
o: You are on a collision course — slow down and be ready to yield
It is travelling at your speed on a parallel road, so it will pass safely
It has stopped and is waiting for you
It will pass behind you
ex: If the other vehicle stays in the same position in your view, you're on a collision course. Start slowing and be prepared to yield or stop. Turn your head — peripheral vision misses it.

q: To steer straight on the highway, where should you look?
o: About 12 seconds directly ahead
At the centre line just in front of your hood, to stay in your lane
At the edge of the road
At the vehicle directly in front
ex: You steer where you look. To steer straight, look about 12 seconds directly ahead of where you are sitting.

q: When should you check your instruments on the highway?
o: On a straight stretch, with gates open and no hazards ahead
While driving through a curve, when steering is steady
Whenever you approach an intersection or a light
Every few seconds, whatever the traffic is doing around you
ex: Even checking your speed takes 1.5 seconds. Check instruments on a straight stretch with your gates open and no real or potential hazards ahead.

q: In city traffic you can't control your rear and side gates. What should you do?
o: Drop back and double the gap ahead to five or six seconds
Speed up to get out of the heavy traffic quickly
Keep changing lanes until all four gates are open
Keep exactly a three-second gap and hold your lane
ex: Never drive with fewer than two gates open. If you can't control the rear and side gates, drop back and double your following distance to five or six seconds.

q: How should your head restraint be adjusted?
o: Its top level with the top of your head
Its top level with your neck
As low as possible, so it does not block the view behind
Its top level with your ears
ex: Adjust the head restraint so the top edge is level with the top of your head — never lower — to reduce whiplash injury.

q: Who is legally responsible for a 14-year-old passenger wearing a seatbelt?
o: The driver
The passenger
The passenger's parent, even if not in the car
No one — it's only recommended
ex: Drivers are legally responsible for passengers under 16 using seatbelts and child seats. Passengers 16 and older are responsible for themselves.

q: Children under what age must ride in an approved car seat or booster seat?
o: Under seven years old
Under five years old
Under nine years old
Under 12 years old
ex: Children under seven must be in correctly installed car seats or boosters, usually until they're about seven and over 36 kg (80 lb.).

q: Why should children never ride in the front seat of a car with a passenger airbag?
o: The force of the airbag can critically injure or kill a small child
Airbags don't deploy at all when a child is in the front seat
Children distract the driver more when they sit in front
It's only a risk in crashes at over 100 km/h
ex: The force of an airbag deploying is enough to critically injure or kill an infant or small child. Airbags inflate in crashes over 16 km/h.

q: How should the lap part of a seatbelt be worn?
o: Low and snug over the pelvis
Across the stomach, loosely
Behind your back with the shoulder belt
Over the thighs, near the knees
ex: Put the lap belt low over your pelvis and pull it snug. Shoulder belts should never be worn behind your back or under your arm.

q: What are the two correct hand positions on the steering wheel?
o: '9 and 3' or '8 and 4'
'10 and 2' or '12 and 6'
'11 and 1' or '7 and 5'
'12 o'clock' with one hand
ex: There are two correct hand positions: '9 and 3' and '8 and 4'. A hand at the top of the wheel can be forced into your face by the airbag.

q: Which foot should you brake with?
o: Always your right foot
Your left foot, to react faster
Either foot
Left foot in an automatic, right in a manual
ex: Your left foot braces against the firewall for stability, so you can't use it to brake. Always brake with your right foot.

q: Your vehicle has a back-up camera. How should you back up?
o: Use the camera and mirrors, but turn your head and look out the rear window
Rely on the camera — it shows everything behind the vehicle
Use only the side mirrors and the camera screen
Back up quickly so the camera image stays sharp
ex: Back-up cameras don't capture everything. Always turn your head to look out the rear window and check all directions.

q: An oil or engine warning light comes on while driving. What should you do?
o: Find out the cause as soon as it is safely possible
Ignore it until your next oil change
Keep driving — it usually turns off by itself
Turn the engine off immediately in traffic
ex: Should an engine or oil warning light come on, determine the cause as soon as safely possible. Driving with a warning light on may damage the vehicle.

q: Which is allowed for a vehicle?
o: Securing all cargo so it cannot fall off
Passengers riding in a trailer on a short trip
Aftermarket tint on the front side windows
A passenger sitting between the driver and the door
ex: All material carried must be securely contained or tied down. Passengers may not ride in a trailer or between the driver and the door; aftermarket tint isn't allowed on the windshield or front side windows.

q: May you smoke in a vehicle with children in it?
o: No — it is illegal to smoke while children are in the vehicle
Yes, as long as at least one window is open for fresh air
Yes, if all the children are older than 12
Yes, but only when driving on the highway
ex: Vehicles with children in them are non-smoking areas; it's illegal to smoke while children are in the vehicle.

q: Why do you turn your front wheels when parking on a hill?
o: So the vehicle rolls into the curb, or off the road, if it starts to roll
So the vehicle will be easier to pull out into traffic later on
So other drivers can see that you are legally parked
To keep the tires from wearing unevenly on the slope
ex: Turn the wheels so that if the vehicle rolls, it rolls into the curb and stops — or, with no curb, off the road. Apply the parking brake whenever you park on a slope.

q: Before parallel parking, how much longer than your vehicle should the space be?
o: At least 2 m longer
At least 1 m longer
At least 3 m longer
Exactly the length of your vehicle
ex: Check that you have at least 2 m more than the length of your vehicle.

q: In a parking lot with 90-degree stalls, what is recommended?
o: Back into the stall, unless prohibited
Drive in forward and back out later
Park across two stalls for room
Back in only at night
ex: Backing into a 90-degree stall is recommended: the front-end swing happens in the aisle, you back into a known-clear space, and you get an excellent view driving out.

q: You park a manual transmission car. What gear should it be left in?
o: In first gear, not neutral
In neutral with the parking brake
In reverse only on flat ground
In the highest gear
ex: When parking a manual vehicle, make sure it's in first gear, not neutral, before leaving it.

q: How do you enter a freeway?
o: Speed up in the acceleration lane to match freeway traffic, then merge
Stop at the end of the ramp and wait for a big gap
Merge slowly at the start of the lane so freeway traffic can adjust
Use the shoulder to wait for a gap, then merge
ex: Increase speed in the acceleration lane until it matches the vehicles on the freeway. Merging at less than freeway speeds can be dangerous.

q: Where should you slow down when leaving a freeway?
o: In the deceleration lane, not on the freeway
On the freeway itself, before you reach the start of the exit
On the exit ramp's curve only
At the end of the ramp, at the stop sign
ex: Signal and move into the deceleration lane, then slow down there — not on the freeway. You're likely to underestimate your speed.

q: You missed your exit on a freeway. What should you do?
o: Continue to the next interchange and come back
Stop on the shoulder and back up carefully to the exit
Make a U-turn across the median
Stop in the lane and signal
ex: If you miss an exit, don't stop or back up on the freeway. Continue to the next interchange and return.

q: Your car starts having trouble on the freeway. What should you do?
o: Pull onto the shoulder as far right as possible and turn on your hazards
Stop in your lane right away and switch on your hazard lights
Keep driving at speed until the car stalls by itself
Stop on the left shoulder, next to the median
ex: At the first sign of trouble, pull onto the nearest shoulder as far right as possible and turn on your hazard lights. Never stop on the travelled portion of the freeway.

q: When should you NOT use cruise control?
o: On wet or slippery roads, in cities and in variable traffic
On long, dry and open highways where traffic is light
When traffic is light and moving at a steady speed
On divided highways in daytime and good weather
ex: Don't use cruise control in urban areas, on wet or slippery roads, in traffic with variable speed or where vision is restricted.

q: What is the most important part of driving a curve or corner?
o: Slow down before you get to it
Brake hard in the middle of the curve
Accelerate into the curve
Look at the outside edge of the curve
ex: The most important part is to slow down before the curve. Brake in a straight line, then ease through it.

q: You are driving on a gravel road toward a hill or blind curve. Where should you be?
o: Right of centre, to leave room for unseen oncoming vehicles
In the centre of the road, where the gravel is packed hardest
On the left, where you can see further
On the shoulder, at slow speed
ex: Even though the main path on gravel is often in the centre, stay right of centre approaching hills and blind curves.

q: You meet a large truck or farm equipment on a gravel road. What should you do?
o: Slow down and pull as far right as possible
Speed up to pass through its dust quickly
Keep to the centre and flash your lights so they move over
Stop in the middle of the road
ex: When meeting large trucks or farm equipment, slow down and pull as far to the right as possible. You may have to stop.

q: Ice looks the same at -2 °C and -22 °C. At which temperature is it more slippery?
o: At -2 °C, the warmer temperature
At -22 °C, the colder temperature
It is equally slippery
It depends only on the tires
ex: Icy roads look the same at -2 °C or -22 °C, but are far more slippery at the warmer temperature.

q: In winter, how low should you let your gas tank get?
o: Not below half full
Not below a quarter
Until the warning light comes on
It doesn't matter in winter
ex: One of the winter temptations to resist: letting your gas tank drop below half full.

q: You are stranded in a winter blizzard. What should you do?
o: Stay with your vehicle and keep the exhaust pipe clear
Walk to the nearest farm for help before the snow gets deeper
Run the engine all night with windows closed
Leave the vehicle once the snow stops falling
ex: Always stay with your vehicle. Keep calm, open a downwind window slightly, keep the exhaust pipe clear and run the engine only for some heat. Many people die walking for help.

q: Driving a curve on a slippery surface, how do you position your vehicle?
o: Toward the inside of the lane before the curve, then gradually across
Toward the outside of the lane before the curve, then hold that line
In the exact centre of the lane all the way through
On the shoulder, where the surface has more traction
ex: On a slippery curve, reduce speed and position toward the inside of the lane before the turn, then gradually steer across the lane. This lessens sideways force.

q: How do you use ABS brakes in an emergency stop?
o: Press the brake firmly and hold it; don't pump
Pump the brake quickly several times
Press lightly and release when the pedal pulses
Brake with both feet for more force
ex: With ABS, press the brake firmly and don't release until stopped. Don't pump — the ABS does it for you. Pedal pulsing and noise are normal.

q: On gravel, slush or snow, how does stopping with ABS compare to conventional brakes?
o: Allow a longer stopping distance with ABS
ABS always stops you in a shorter distance on loose surfaces
The distance is exactly the same
ABS lets you stop almost instantly
ex: Allow a longer stopping distance with ABS on gravel, slush and snow — the rolling tires 'float' on the loose layer.

q: You must choose between braking and steering to avoid an obstacle. What does the handbook recommend?
o: Steer — you can steer around it in a shorter distance than stopping
Brake — braking in a straight line is always safer than steering
Brake and steer hard at the same time without ABS
Neither — sound the horn and hold your course
ex: If your choice is between braking or steering, choose to steer: you can steer around an obstacle in a shorter distance than it takes to stop.

q: In an emergency or a skid, where should you look?
o: Where you want to go — and steer there
At the object you are trying to avoid
At the instrument panel
Down at the road just in front
ex: Look where you want to go and steer there. Don't look at the tree you want to avoid — look at the gap you want to get through.

q: Your car skids because you braked too hard. What should you do?
o: Take your foot off the brake, look where you want to go and steer
Press the brake even harder until the car stops
Accelerate firmly so the wheels regain their grip
Turn the wheel sharply away from the direction of the skid
ex: For any skid caused by braking: shift to neutral (declutch), remove your foot from the brake, look where you want to go and steer there.

q: Your car skids from too much acceleration on a slippery road. What should you do?
o: Ease off the accelerator, don't touch the brake, look and steer where you want to go
Brake hard right away so that the drive wheels stop spinning
Accelerate even more to power out of the skid
Switch on cruise control so the speed stays even
ex: Shift to neutral (declutch), take your foot off the accelerator, look where you want to go and steer there. Do not touch the brake.

q: Your right wheels drop onto a soft shoulder. What should you do?
o: Steer straight along the shoulder and slow gradually, then return gently
Jerk the wheel to the left at once to get back on the road quickly
Brake hard right away while the wheels are on the shoulder
Accelerate so the car climbs back onto the pavement
ex: Don't jerk the wheel or brake hard. Steer straight along the shoulder, slow gradually, then when clear, steer gently back and straighten out.

q: Your car is going into a ditch. What should you do to avoid a rollover?
o: Drive down the ditch, stay off the brake, steer gently
Turn sharply back toward the road before the car goes any deeper
Brake as hard as you can
Accelerate to climb out of the ditch
ex: Don't brake hard, turn violently or try to get back on the road. Drive down the ditch — the main cause of rollovers is returning to the road too early.

q: A front tire blows out. What should you do?
o: Hold the wheel firmly, ease off the accelerator and brake gently
Brake hard immediately so the car stops as fast as possible
Steer quickly toward the shoulder before slowing
Accelerate a little to keep the car stable
ex: Don't over-react. Hold the wheel firmly, look where you want to go, ease off the accelerator and brake gently, then steer off the road.

q: Your brake pedal goes almost to the floor. What does the handbook advise?
o: Keep pressing — it still has power — and use the parking brake carefully
Pump the brake pedal rapidly to build up pressure again
Turn the engine off right away to slow the car
Shift straight into park while still moving
ex: Modern brakes have two circuits; keep pushing harder. Use the parking brake gently to avoid locking the rear wheels. Don't pump the brakes.

q: Your accelerator sticks. What should you do first?
o: Shift to neutral (or declutch), then slow down and pull over
Turn the key off immediately, even while still at highway speed
Pump the accelerator pedal to try to free it
Brake hard while the car is still in gear
ex: Don't panic. Shift to neutral (or declutch), slow down, pull over and stop. Then turn the key off and try to free the pedal.

q: Your headlights suddenly go out at night. What should you do?
o: Slow down, keep your course, pull over and stop
Brake hard and stop right away in your lane
Keep driving using the road edge
Speed up to reach a lit area
ex: Immediately slow down to keep your original course, pull over and stop. Check the switches; if they don't work, use parking or hazard lights.

q: A deer suddenly appears in front of you. What should you do?
o: Brake firmly and stay in control; avoid swerving
Swerve sharply around it, toward the side it came from
Speed up so it runs away
Swerve into the ditch to be safe
ex: If an animal surprises you, brake firmly and stay in control. Avoid swerving — you may turn into oncoming traffic or roll into the ditch.

q: A collision with an animal is unavoidable. Where should you aim?
o: At the spot the animal came from, not where it is going
At where the animal is going, so that you pass behind it
Directly at the middle of the animal's body
Into the ditch on the right side of the road
ex: Aim at the spot where the animal came from, try for a glancing blow, and let up on the brake just before impact so the front rises slightly.

q: When are collisions with wildlife most likely?
o: At dawn and dusk
At noon
Between midnight and 3 a.m., when traffic is lightest
In the middle of the afternoon
ex: The peak times for wildlife collisions are dawn and dusk. Risk is also high in May–June and in late fall and early winter.

q: Animals are being herded across the road. What should you do?
o: Slow down and wait for the herder to signal it's safe; don't honk
Sound your horn so the animals move off the road faster
Drive slowly and steadily through the middle of the herd
Pass the herd on the shoulder while keeping your distance
ex: Slow down and wait for the herder or rider to move the animals and indicate it's safe. Don't use your horn — it may panic the animals.

q: After a collision, when should injured people be moved?
o: Only if they are in danger of drowning, suffocating, burning or electrocution
Always, so that they can be taken out of the damaged cars quickly
Once they tell you they feel fine and want to get out
Only after you have photographed the collision scene
ex: Injured persons should be moved only if they are in danger of drowning, suffocating, burning or being electrocuted.

q: Which collision must be reported to police immediately?
o: One where a vehicle must be towed from the scene
Any collision at all, even a small scrape in a parking lot
Only collisions with injuries
Only collisions on highways
ex: Report immediately to police: injury or death, hit and run, an impaired driver, an out-of-province vehicle, or where a vehicle must be towed.

q: Your vehicle touches a power line in a collision. What should you do?
o: Stay in the vehicle and call for help
Get out quickly and run away
Touch the ground with one foot before getting out
Push the line off with a branch
ex: If your vehicle contacts a power line, stay in it and call SaskPower or 9-1-1. Exit only if it's on fire: jump clear with feet together and hop at least 10 m.

q: After a collision, what must you give the other drivers involved?
o: Your name, address, driver's licence number and plate number
Only your insurance company's name and phone number
Nothing until police arrive
A written statement of who was at fault
ex: You must provide your name, address, driver's licence number and plate number to others involved. Don't admit fault before talking with your adjuster.

q: You come upon a collision at night. How do you protect the scene?
o: Set flares well away from the scene and turn on hazard lights
Park in the middle of the road to block traffic from the scene
Turn off all lights to avoid glare
Wait in your car until police arrive
ex: Warn approaching traffic with flares well away from the scene or people signalling at each end, and turn on the hazard lights of undamaged vehicles.

q: What is an early warning sign of fatigue?
o: You stop moving your eyes and stare straight ahead
You start checking your mirrors and gauges more often than usual
Your speed becomes very steady
You notice more signs than usual
ex: An early warning sign of fatigue is not looking as far ahead as you should — you stare straight ahead instead of using your search pattern.

q: An aggressive driver is behind you. What is the safest thing to do?
o: Pull over and let them pass
Make eye contact so they calm down
Brake to slow them down
Speed up to stay ahead
ex: Avoid eye contact with an aggressive driver. The best thing you can do is pull over and let that person pass.

q: You are very upset after bad news. What does the handbook advise?
o: Don't drive — arrange for someone else to drive
Drive slowly with music on
Drive, but only on roads you know well, and below the limit
Drive if you take a short break first
ex: Emotional or physical stress distracts you from the thinking part of driving. If you're under stress, don't drive — arrange to be driven by someone else.
